A declining equity percentage can still leave more dollars exposed as retirement saving grows

Follow an original allocation path alongside contribution-only portfolio values, then compare the dollar effect of the same equity decline at different checkpoints.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a planned allocation path while adding new saving

Original contribution-only allocation illustration. The portfolio starts with selected capital and receives equal year-end contributions. Every asset earns zero return before the separate shock comparison, so the balance is capital plus deposits rather than an investment forecast. The planned equity share changes linearly between the selected endpoints; each year-end portfolio is reset to that mix without transaction costs or tax. The remaining allocation is called other assets. In the isolated one-time shock, only equities fall and other assets do not change; that is a scenario assumption, not a claim that other assets are safe. Start, peak-exposure and target shocks are separate snapshots, not sequential losses on one path. No withdrawals, inflation, fees, rebalancing restrictions, actual fund holdings or adequate-retirement-income assessment is included. A target-date fund’s actual glide path may differ; the model stops at the selected target.

The central idea

Read the planned percentage beside the portfolio amount. A lower equity share can reduce a snapshot’s percentage loss while a larger account produces a greater dollar loss.

01

An allocation path describes a mix, not an income guarantee

A target-date strategy can change its investment mix as a goal approaches. The SEC’s March 2025 target-date-fund bulletin explains glide paths and notes that funds with the same target date can differ. Its discussion concerns U.S.-registered mutual funds and ETFs; it is general context here, not a description of a Canadian plan or a particular product.

The charts use an independently authored allocation path. No actual fund, expected return or recommended equity weight is selected. The purpose is to separate a percentage allocation from the dollars to which that percentage applies.

That distinction matters when saving continues. An account can become more conservatively allocated by one percentage measure while its equity amount remains larger than it was earlier. Neither the mix nor the amount alone tells us whether a retirement income plan is adequate.

02

Specify the endpoint, contributions and reset convention

The default begins with CAD 100,000 and adds CAD 20,000 at each year-end for thirty years. All assets earn zero return before the separate shock exercise. The total therefore reaches CAD 700,000 entirely through new saving, without any assumption about market performance.

The planned equity share falls in a straight line from 80% at the start to 35% at the target. The other-asset share is the remainder. At year fifteen, halfway through this authored path, the planned equity share is 57.5%.

Each year-end portfolio is reset to that mix after the contribution, without tax or transaction costs. This is a simplifying allocation convention, not a simulation of actual trades or a promise that new deposits alone can achieve every target weight. The related rebalancing guide addresses the constraints of changing a mix using contributions without sales.

03

Multiply the percentage by the portfolio it describes

At the start, 80% of CAD 100,000 is CAD 80,000 in equities. At the target, 35% of CAD 700,000 is CAD 245,000. The percentage has fallen by 45 percentage points, yet the equity amount is a little over three times its starting level.

The path also shows why endpoints are not the whole story. In this default, the largest whole-year equity amount occurs at year twenty-four. The portfolio then contains CAD 580,000, and its planned equity share is 44%, giving CAD 255,200 in equities.

Equity dollars subsequently fall to CAD 245,000 by the target as the allocation reduction outweighs the additional saving. This peak follows from the chosen contribution and allocation formulas. It is not a forecast that a real account will peak at that time or that a fund follows this straight-line schedule.

04

A smaller percentage loss can accompany a larger dollar loss

Apply a hypothetical 30% decline to equity values while leaving other assets unchanged. At the starting snapshot, the modeled change is negative CAD 24,000: 30% of CAD 80,000. That equals 24% of the initial total portfolio.

At the target snapshot, the modeled change is negative CAD 73,500: 30% of CAD 245,000. It equals 10.5% of the larger portfolio. The portfolio-level percentage effect is smaller, but the dollar effect is greater. The peak-equity snapshot produces a CAD 76,560 decline under the same isolated assumption.

These are independent snapshot comparisons. The model does not apply all three losses in succession or reduce the contribution path by them. Other assets staying unchanged is an explicit stress assumption, not a claim that bonds, cash substitutes or other holdings cannot lose value.

05

Keep the exposure question separate from the funding question

The matrix varies the target equity share and annual saving while retaining the selected capital, horizon and equity-decline assumption. Every cell shows the magnitude of the hypothetical target-snapshot loss in Canadian dollars.

Saving more can increase that dollar amount because more capital is present. This does not make saving less a stronger plan. A smaller portfolio may show a smaller modeled loss while providing fewer resources for the goal. Likewise, reducing the equity share changes exposure but does not itself determine an achievable return or sufficient retirement income.

The starting equity share changes the interim path and its possible peak. It does not change the endpoint matrix, which uses the selected ending share and contribution-only ending balance. Read the percentage, balance and cash-flow purpose together rather than interpreting a single smaller cell as an improvement.

06

Review the actual path and the money that will be needed

For a real plan, identify the expected use dates, planned contributions, accessible reserves and other income sources. A dollar loss can have different consequences depending on whether withdrawals begin next month or the goal has flexibility. This contribution-only example calculates neither withdrawal capacity nor recovery time.

Read a fund’s actual allocation policy, fees and full glide path. Some paths continue changing after the named date; this model stops at its selected target. The SEC bulletin also states that target-date mutual funds and ETFs do not guarantee sufficient retirement income. A calendar label cannot replace a review of the whole plan.

The charts exclude investment growth, inflation, withdrawals, fees, tax and trading restrictions. Their value is a transparent check of the relationship among saving, percentages and dollars. Use them to frame an exposure question before making a goal-specific decision, without treating an authored path or shock as a forecast or a suitable allocation.
